content: When there is a high degree of variability or strong reasons suggesting that the recommended course of action is unlikely to be accepted, it is more appropriate to issue a conditional recommendation rather than a strong one. Lower costs, whether monetary, related to infrastructure, equipment, or human resources, or greater cost-effectiveness, are factors that contribute to a strong recommendation. If an intervention is feasible and can be implemented in a setting where it is expected to have the greatest impact, a strong recommendation is warranted. If a recommendation is likely to improve access to an intervention for those most in need, it is more likely to be classified as a strong recommendation. The GRADE approach defines four levels of certainty of evidence: high, moderate, low, and very low. Based on the certainty of evidence, the strength of a recommendation can be categorized as either strong or conditional. For high certainty of evidence, there is a very high level of confidence that the true effect is close to the estimated effect. For moderate certainty, there is moderate confidence in the estimated effect, but the true effect may differ substantially. For low certainty, confidence in the estimated effect is limited, and the true effect may be significantly different. For very low certainty, there is very little confidence in the estimated effect, and any estimate of effect is highly uncertain. The WHO convened two virtual technical consultations with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) in December 2020 and March 2021. During this period, the Guideline Steering Group (GSG) also met three times. The December 2020 GDG meeting involved reviewing background materials, presenting the systematic review protocol, and discussing preliminary findings from analyses on values, preferences, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness. The March 2021 GDG meeting included the presentation of final systematic review findings and supporting evidence. At the start of the March 2021 meeting, the WHO and GDG agreed that the goal for decision-making would be to reach consensus, defined as group agreement. If consensus could not be achieved, a vote requiring at least 60% approval would be necessary to finalize the recommendation. During the March meeting, the GDG, facilitated by a methodologist, reviewed systematic review evidence and supplementary evidence on values, preferences, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness. The group also discussed evidence on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing (HCVST) and additional evidence on HIV Self-Testing (HIVST). The GDG determined that evidence from HIVST was highly applicable to HCVST, as similar outcomes and effects were anticipated, with overlapping populations in many settings. Following these discussions, the GDG reached consensus on the direction, strength, and wording of the recommendation. Additional remarks were added to address key considerations for implementation. The WHO subsequently drafted the full guidelines and circulated them electronically to the GDG, GSG, and External Review Group (ERG) for comments and feedback. All responses were reviewed and addressed as appropriate in the final draft. The final guidelines will be published electronically on the WHO website, along with web annexes.
